claim: Hematopoiesis is regulated by the bone marrow (BM) stroma.
source: Hematopoiesis is regulated by the bone marrow (BM) stroma.
evidence: This is a well-established scientific consensus in the field of hematology.

claim: Cellular identities and functions of the different BM stromal elements in humans remain poorly defined.
source: However, cellular identities and functions of the different BM stromal elements in humans remain poorly defined.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The study systematically characterized the human non-hematopoietic BM stromal compartment based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq).
source: Based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), we systematically characterized the human non-hematopoietic BM stromal compartment
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study investigated stromal cell regulation principles based on RNA velocity analysis using scVelo.
source: we investigated stromal cell regulation principles based on the RNA velocity analysis using scVelo
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methods used.

claim: The study investigated interactions between human BM stromal cells and hematopoietic cells based on ligand-receptor (LR) expression using CellPhoneDB.
source: studied the interactions between the human BM stromal cells and hematopoietic cells based on ligand-receptor (LR) expression using CellPhoneDB.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical methods used.

claim: scRNAseq led to the identification of six transcriptionally and functionally distinct stromal cell populations.
source: scRNAseq led to the identification of six transcriptionally and functionally distinct stromal cell populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Stromal cell differentiation hierarchy was recapitulated based on RNA velocity analysis and in vitro proliferation capacities and differentiation potentials.
source: Stromal cell differentiation hierarchy was recapitulated based on RNA velocity analysis and in vitro proliferation capacities and differentiation potentials.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on computational and experimental data.

claim: Potential key factors that might govern the transition from stem and progenitor cells to fate-committed cells were identified.
source: Potential key factors that might govern the transition from stem and progenitor cells to fate-committed cells were identified.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on computational analysis.

claim: In situ localization analysis demonstrated that different stromal cells were localized in different niches in the bone marrow.
source: In situ localization analysis demonstrated that different stromal cells were localized in different niches in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on immunofluorescence staining data.

claim: In silico cell-cell communication analysis predicted that different stromal cell types might regulate hematopoiesis through distinct mechanisms.
source: In silico cell-cell communication analysis further predicted that different stromal cell types might regulate hematopoiesis through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is a prediction based on computational analysis of ligand-receptor interactions.

claim: Bone marrow (BM) is the principal site of hematopoiesis in adult humans.
source: Bone marrow (BM) is the principal site of hematopoiesis in adult humans.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: In the BM, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their progenies are contained in specialized microenvironments which regulate HSC maintenance and differentiation.
source: In the BM, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their progenies are contained in specialized microenvironments which regulate HSC maintenance and differentiation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Understanding of the BM hematopoietic microenvironment (HME) has evolved considerably over the past decade through landmark studies in mice.
source: Our understanding of the BM hematopoietic microenvironment (HME) has evolved considerably over the past decade through a number of landmark studies that have identified the cellular identity, anatomy, and functions of different murine HME components (Baryawno et al., 2019; Tikhonova et al., 2019; Wolock et al., 2019; Baccin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Skeletal and stromal cell populations, endothelial cells and other non-hematopoietic cells but also differentiated hematopoietic cells have been described as important HME elements in mice.
source: Skeletal and stromal cell populations, endothelial cells and other non-hematopoietic cells but also differentiated hematopoietic cells have been described as important HME elements in mice (Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2008; Urbieta et al., 2010; Yamazaki et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2012; Casanova-Acebes et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Important HME elements in human BM remain poorly defined.
source: In contrast, important HME elements in human BM remain poorly defined, which is due to the fact that the identity and function of the stromal stem/progenitor cells have been difficult to investigate (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: The identity and function of stromal stem/progenitor cells in human BM have been difficult to investigate.
source: In contrast, important HME elements in human BM remain poorly defined, which is due to the fact that the identity and function of the stromal stem/progenitor cells have been difficult to investigate (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Recent studies have provided the first important insights into the complexity of the human BM and the potential diverse functional roles of BM stromal cells.
source: Nevertheless, a number of recent studies have provided the first important insights into the complexity of the human BM and the potential diverse functional roles of BM stromal cells (Chan et al., 2018; de Jong et al., 2021; Triana et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human bone marrow cells were collected from consenting healthy donors by aspiration from the iliac crest.
source: Human bone marrow (BM) cells were collected at the Hematology Department, Skåne University Hospital Lund, Sweden, from consenting healthy donors by aspiration from the iliac crest as described previously (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Bone marrow mononuclear cells (BM-MNC) were isolated by density gradient centrifugation.
source: Bone marrow mononuclear cells (BM-MNC) were isolated by density gradient centrifugation (LSM 1077 Lymphocyte, PAA, Pasching, Austria).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: The use of human samples was approved by the Regional Ethics Review Board in Lund, Sweden.
source: The use of human samples was approved by the Regional Ethics Review Board in Lund, Sweden.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: The dataset was comprised of 25,067 cells with a median of 856 genes and 2937 UMIs per cell.
source: In total, our dataset was comprised of 25,067 cells (median of 856 genes and 2937 UMIs per cell, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the scRNAseq dataset.

claim: The dataset formed 42 clusters corresponding to distinct cell types and differentiation stages.
source: In total, our dataset was comprised of 25,067 cells (median of 856 genes and 2937 UMIs per cell, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) which formed 42 clusters corresponding to distinct cell types and differentiation stages, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F, Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: scRNAseq analysis of CD45low/-CD235a- cells captured several hematopoietic cell types including a cluster of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) enriched for CD34 expression.
source: As expected (Boulais et al., 2018; Baryawno et al., 2019), scRNAseq analysis of CD45low/-CD235a- cells captured several hematopoietic cell types including a cluster of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) enriched for CD34 expression and other HSPC markers (PROM1, CRHBP, AVP, MLLT3, FAM30A, GATA1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, and Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis supported by citations.

claim: Non-hematopoietic cells including stromal cells, endothelial cells, KRT5-enriched basal cell-like cluster, and a cluster of cells enriched for neuronal markers expression could be clearly identified.
source: Importantly, non-hematopoietic cells including stromal cells as well as non-stromal cells, such as endothelial cells (cluster 28), KRT5-enriched basal cell-like cluster (cluster 0), and a cluster of cells enriched for neuronal markers expression (cluster 39) could be clearly identified (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: Nine stromal clusters were identified after CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ cells were included in the analysis.
source: Of note, following the exclusion of hematopoietic cells and the other non-stromal cell types, we identified nine stromal clusters (clusters 3, 5, 6, 8, 16, 23, 29, 37, 38, Figure 1B and C), which only became detectable after CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ cells were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The nine stromal progenitor populations shared a unique gene expression profile, including both well-established stromal markers as well as novel markers.
source: The nine stromal progenitor populations shared a unique gene expression profile, including both well-established stromal markers as well as novel markers (Supplementary file 2; Supplementary file 4; Supplementary file 7; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The stromal clusters were annotated as multipotent stromal stem cells (MSSCs), highly adipocytic gene-expressing progenitors (HAGEPs), balanced progenitors, pre-osteoblasts, osteochondrogenic progenitors (OCs), and pre-fibroblasts.
source: The stromal clusters were then annotated based on their expression of previously reported BM stromal markers (Churchman et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014), which allowed us to discriminate six different cell types, that is multipotent stromal stem cells (MSSCs), highly adipocytic gene-expressing progenitors (HAGEPs), balanced progenitors, pre-osteoblasts, osteochondrogenic progenitors (OCs), and pre-fibroblasts (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: Cluster 3 was annotated as MSSCs with multi-lineage differentiation capacity based on its high expression of stromal markers and genes indicating both adipogenic and osteogenic differentiation capacities.
source: Cluster 3 was annotated as MSSCs with multi-lineage differentiation capacity based on its high expression of stromal markers (CXCL12, LEPR, DCN, PTGDS) and genes indicating both adipogenic (CEBPD, LPL, PLIN1, ADIPOQ, CCL2, PPARG) and osteogenic (GAS6, FBN1, ALPL, RUNX1, SPARCL1, CDH11) differentiation capacities (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: The annotation of cluster 3 as MSSCs was confirmed by velocity analysis.
source: The annotation of cluster 3 as MSSCs was further confirmed by velocity analysis as shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is a finding from the RNA velocity analysis.

claim: Cluster 5 was termed as highly adipocytic gene-expressing progenitors (HAGEPs) based on expression of adipogenic differentiation markers and stress-related transcription factors.
source: Cells in cluster 5 expressed adipogenic differentiation markers as well as a group of stress-related transcription factors such as FOS, FOSB, JUNB and EGR1, some of which have been shown to mark bone marrow adipogenic progenitors (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Ambrosi et al., 2017). Osteogenic differentiation markers were also expressed but at considerably lower levels compared to adipogenic genes (Figure 2D). Thus, cluster 5 was termed as highly adipocytic gene-expressing progenitors (HAGEPs).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression and supported by a citation.

claim: Cluster 16 showed similar expression levels of adipogenic and osteogenic markers and was annotated as balanced progenitors.
source: Cluster 16 on the other hand, showed similar expression levels of adipogenic and osteogenic markers and was therefore annotated as balanced progenitors (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: A gradual increase of more mature osteogenic markers was observed from cluster 5 to cluster 16 and to cluster 38.
source: We observed a gradual increase of more mature osteogenic markers such as RUNX1, CDH11, EBF1, and EBF3 from cluster 5 to cluster 16 and to cluster 38 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: Cluster 38 was denoted as pre-osteoblasts.
source: Accordingly, cluster 38 was denoted as pre-osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: Clusters 29 and 23 were characterized by prominent expression of osteochondrogenic markers and were assigned as osteochondrogenic progenitors (OCs).
source: Clusters 29 and 23 were characterized by prominent expression of osteochondrogenic markers including BGLAP, CHAD, SPP1(OPN), RUNX2, CDH11, CDH2, IBSP (BSP), and SPARC (Figure 2B and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Hence, these two clusters were assigned as osteochondrogenic progenitors (OCs).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: Clusters 6, 37 and 8 expressed adipogenic and osteogenic markers as well as hematopoiesis-related markers and S100 genes, and were annotated as pre-fibroblasts.
source: While both adipogenic and osteogenic marker expression was detected in clusters 6, 37 and 8, they also expressed several hematopoiesis-related markers such as SRGN, CD52, CD37, CD48, and PTPRC (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and D). Furthermore, S100 genes, which encode a group of calcium-binding cytosolic proteins, were expressed almost exclusively in cluster 8 (Figure 2B and F), and the previously reported murine fibroblast markers, S100A4 and S100 A6 (Słomnicki and Leśniak, 2010, Baryawno et al., 2019) were highly expressed in all three clusters. Based on this expression pattern, clusters 6, 37, and 8 were subsequently annotated as pre-fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression and supported by citations.

claim: RNA velocity analysis predicted that the MSSC cluster has two main developmental directions.
source: RNA velocity analysis predicted that the MSSC cluster has two main developmental directions (Figure 3A') with the first originating from MSSCs (cluster 3) and moving towards HAGEPs (cluster 5), followed by OCs (cluster 29) and terminating at the pre-osteoblast cluster (cluster 38). The second main differentiation path, which also originated from MSSCs (cluster 3), was directed towards balanced progenitors and ended at either the pre-osteoblasts or the pre-fibroblasts stage.
evidence: This is a finding from the RNA velocity analysis.

claim: Latent time analysis identified MSSCs as the root cell population and placed pre-osteoblasts close to the terminal state of differentiation.
source: Latent time analysis, which represents the cell's internal clock and approximates the real time experienced by cells as they differentiate, also identified MSSCs as the root cell population and placed pre-osteoblasts close to the terminal state of differentiation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the latent time analysis.

claim: scVelo identified potential key driver genes that govern cellular state transitions, including CSTA, B2M, CXCL12, and COL1A2 for transitions within the MSSC cluster.
source: A group of genes, including CSTA, B2M, CXCL12, and COL1A2 was found to drive the gradual and subtle cellular state transitions within the MSSC cluster (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the scVelo analysis.

claim: Known adipogenic genes such as CEBPD together with LEPR, CTSC, LMNA, KLF6, and EGR1 were identified to play important roles in the transition from MSSCs to HAGEPs.
source: Known adipogenic genes such as CEBPD (Cao et al., 1991) together with LEPR, CTSC, LMNA, KLF6, and EGR1 were identified to play important roles in the transition from MSSCs to HAGEPs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the scVelo analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Novel drivers (NFKBIA, RBM3, TUBA1A, and DDX24) and reported genes such as ANXA1 were identified to serve as critical genes in the transition from HAGEPs to OCs.
source: Furthermore, both novel drivers (NFKBIA, RBM3, TUBA1A, and DDX24), as well as reported genes such as ANXA1 (Headland et al., 2015), were identified to serve as critical genes in the transition from HAGEPs to OCs (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the scVelo analysis supported by a citation.

claim: VCAN was identified as one of the crucial genes for the transition from MSSCs to balanced progenitors and pre-osteoblasts.
source: VCAN expression has been demonstrated to correlate with bone formation in rats (Nakamura et al., 2005). Accordingly, VCAN was identified as one of the crucial genes for the transition from MSSCs to balanced progenitors and even to the pre-osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the scVelo analysis supported by a citation.

claim: The nine stromal subsets could be assigned to three main groups (Group A, B, and C) based on expression patterns of stromal markers, osteochondrogenic genes, and fibroblastic markers.
source: Based on the expression patterns of stromal markers, osteochondrogenic genes, and fibroblastic markers, the nine stromal subsets could be further assigned to three main groups (Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Group A cells (clusters 3, 5, 16, 38), which included MSSCs, HAGEPs, balanced progenitors, and pre-osteoblasts, showed high expression of stromal markers, adipogenic and osteogenic differentiation genes. Group B cells (clusters 29 and 23), annotated as OCs (Figure 2), demonstrated exclusive and specific expressions of osteochondro-lineage markers. Group C cells (clusters 6, 37, and 8), assigned as pre-fibroblasts (Figure 2), exhibited characteristic expression of a group of S100 genes, such as S100A4, S100A6, S100A8, and S100A9.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis based on marker gene expression.

claim: Surface marker gene expression differed between groups A, B, and C.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, surface marker gene expression differed between groups A, B, and C.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: Group B cells showed exclusive expression of NCAM1 and CD9.
source: Group B cells showed exclusive expression of NCAM1 and CD9, which were considerably lower expressed by group A and C cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: Group C cells expressed several surface molecules which are conventionally considered as hematopoietic markers (CD52, CD37, PTPRC, and CD48).
source: Group C cells expressed several surface molecules which are conventionally considered as hematopoietic markers (CD52, CD37, PTPRC, and CD48).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The MSSC population (A1: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81++) had the highest potential to form fibroblastic colonies (CFU-F) and multi-lineage differentiation capacity toward osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes.
source: Functional analysis of sorted cells showed that the MSSC population (A1: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81++) had the highest potential to form fibroblastic colonies (colony-forming units, fibroblast: CFU-F) and multi-lineage differentiation capacity toward osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: HAGEPs (A2: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81+) gave rise to a significant fraction of colonies and showed full in vitro differentiation capacities.
source: Although the CFU-F frequency of HAGEPs (A2: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81+) was lower compared to MSSCs, they still gave rise to a significant fraction of colonies and showed full in vitro differentiation capacities (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: Colony-forming capacities of balanced progenitors, pre-osteoblasts and OCs were considerably lower in comparison with MSSCs and HAGEPs.
source: Colony-forming capacities of balanced progenitors (A3: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81+-), pre-osteoblasts (A4: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1-CD52-CD81-) and OCs (B: CD45low/-CD235a-CD71-CD271+NCAM1+CD52-) were considerably lower in comparison with MSSCs and HAGEPs (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: Pre-fibroblasts (group C) showed the lowest potential to form fibroblastic colonies.
source: Pre-fibroblasts (group C) showed the lowest potential to form fibroblastic colonies (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: The adipogenic potential of pre-fibroblasts was markedly reduced and the pre-fibroblast-derived chondrocyte pellets were smaller compared to the other groups while osteogenic differentiation was normal.
source: Furthermore, the adipogenic potential of pre-fibroblasts was markedly reduced and the pre-fibroblast-derived chondrocyte pellets were smaller compared to the other groups while osteogenic differentiation was normal (Figure 4D), thus indicating a limited differentiation potential of this population.
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: OCs (group B) demonstrated an enhanced capacity to differentiate towards osteoblasts and chondrocytes, however, at the expense of adipogenic potential.
source: OCs (group B) demonstrated an enhanced capacity to differentiate towards osteoblasts and chondrocytes, however, at the expense of adipogenic potential (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: CD271-expressing cells were found in perivascular regions, endosteal regions, and throughout the stroma.
source: As shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E, CD271-expressing cells were found in perivascular regions, endosteal regions, and throughout the stroma.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis.

claim: Perivascular cells surrounding the capillary endothelium and larger vessels primarily expressed CD271 alone.
source: We observed that perivascular cells surrounding the capillary endothelium and larger vessels primarily expressed CD271 alone.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis.

claim: Bone-lining cells proximal to the surface of trabecular bone showed expression of both CD271 and NCAM1.
source: The bone-lining cells proximal to the surface of trabecular bone showed expression of both CD271 and NCAM1, confirming the osteochondrogenic nature of OCs, which correlated very well with the predicted endosteal localizations of murine osteoblasts and chondrocytes (Baccin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis supported by a citation.

claim: CD271/CD81 double-positive cells were localized in bone marrow stromal regions, including both peri-adipocytic and perivascular regions with a considerable fraction being located in close proximity or encircling adipocytes.
source: In contrast to the CD271/NCAM1 double-positive cells, CD271/CD81 double-positive cells were localized in bone marrow stromal regions, including both peri-adipocytic and perivascular regions with a considerable fraction of CD271/CD81 cells being located in close proximity or encircling adipocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis.

claim: Co-staining with CD45 confirmed that perivascular, periadipocytic, and bone-lining cells were CD45 negative.
source: Co-staining with CD45 confirmed that perivascular, periadipocytic, and bone-lining cells were CD45 negative.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis.

claim: A wide range of interactions between stromal cells and hematopoietic cells were identified based on ligand-receptor expression analysis.
source: As shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, we identified a wide range of interactions between stromal cells and hematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Cells belonging to the three stromal groups (A-C) were predicted to have multiple interactions with a large number of hematopoietic cell types, including HSPCs and more mature hematopoietic cells.
source: Generally, cells belonging to the three stromal groups (A-C) were predicted to have multiple interactions with a large number of hematopoietic cell types, including HSPCs and more mature hematopoietic cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Only a few LR pairs were identified between stromal cells and plasma cells.
source: Interestingly, only a few LR pairs were identified between stromal cells and plasma cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: CXCL12 was highly expressed by group A and C stromal cells, especially the MSSC population.
source: CXCL12 was highly expressed by group A and C stromal cells, especially the MSSC population (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is a finding from scRNAseq analysis.

claim: CXCL12-CXCR4 crosstalk was detected in almost all hematopoietic clusters except for erythroid progenitors.
source: CXCL12-CXCR4 crosstalk was detected in almost all hematopoietic clusters except for erythroid progenitors (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: CXCL12-mediated interactions represent one of the major interaction mechanisms between group A and C stromal cells and hematopoietic cells.
source: Furthermore, large dot sizes and high statistical power indicated that CXCL12-mediated interactions represent one of the major interaction mechanisms between these stromal cells and hematopoietic cells (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: SPP1-mediated interactions were predominant in the crosstalk between group B stromal cells (OCs) and hematopoietic cells (except for megakaryocytes).
source: In contrast to the strong contribution of CXCL12-mediated interactions between group A and C stromal cells and hematopoietic cells, SPP1-mediated interactions were predominant in the crosstalk between group B stromal cells (OCs) and hematopoietic cells (except for megakaryocytes), indicating a stromal group-specific interaction (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Interacting partners of SPP1-expressing OCs were erythroid cells, lymphoid progenitors (B, T, NK progenitors) and CD34-enriched HSPC cluster which expressed SPP1 binding partners such as CD44 and PTGER4.
source: Interacting partners of SPP1-expressing OCs were erythroid cells, lymphoid progenitors (B, T, NK progenitors) and CD34-enriched HSPC cluster which expressed SPP1 binding partners such as CD44 and PTGER4 (Figures 5B and 6D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: FACS analysis demonstrated that SPP1 expression was higher in OCs in comparison with MSSCs.
source: Consistent with this, FACS analysis demonstrated that SPP1 expression was higher in OCs in comparison with MSSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis.

claim: In situ staining demonstrated that SPP1-expressing cells were exclusively colocalized endosteally with NCAM1+ OCs.
source: Moreover, in situ staining demonstrated that SPP1-expressing cells were exclusively colocalized endosteally with NCAM1+ OCs (Figure 6E), pointing to a localization-specific regulation.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ staining analysis.

claim: The interplay between erythroid cells and group A and C stromal cells was not dependent on CXCL12-involving interactions as indicated by lacking expression of CXCL12 receptors in erythroid clusters.
source: Unlike the majority of the hematopoietic cells in our dataset, the interplay between erythroid cells and group A and C stromal cells was not dependent on CXCL12-involving interactions as indicated by lacking expression of CXCL12 receptors in erythroid clusters (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Group A and C stromal cells had the potential to interact with erythroid cells through VCAM1-, FN1-, TNC- and PLAUR- involving complexes.
source: CellPhoneDB analysis demonstrated that while group A and C stromal cells had the potential to interact with the erythroid cells through VCAM1-, FN1-, TNC- and PLAUR- involving complexes, the interactions between OCs (group B) and erythroid cells were mainly mediated by SPP1-CD44 (Figures 5B and 6D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: TF (transferrin) was exclusively expressed by all stromal clusters and its corresponding receptors, TFRC and TFR2 were highly expressed by erythroid progenitors.
source: In addition to that, we found that TF (transferrin) was exclusively expressed by all stromal clusters and its corresponding receptors, TFRC and TFR2 were highly expressed by erythroid progenitors (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The crucial stromal cell growth factors PDGFs (PDGFA, PDGFB, and PDGFC) were highly expressed by megakaryocytes while their corresponding receptors (PDGFRA and PDGFRB) were predominantly expressed by stromal cells.
source: Accordingly, we found that the crucial stromal cell growth factors PDGFs (PDGFA, PDGFB, and PDGFC) were highly expressed by megakaryocytes while their corresponding receptors (PDGFRA and PDGFRB) were predominantly expressed by stromal cells (Figure 6G), suggesting interactions through these axes (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from scRNAseq analysis and in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Hematopoietic cells control stromal cells via the TGFB1-EGFR and TGFB1-TGFBR1/2/3 axes.
source: Our analysis also predicted that hematopoietic cells control stromal cells via the TGFB1-EGFR and TGFB1-TGFBR1/2/3 axes (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Oncostatin M (OSM) expression was found in various hematopoietic cell types, indicating a possible regulation of stromal cells through its receptors, OSMR and LIFR.
source: Furthermore, Oncostatin M (OSM) expression was found in various hematopoietic cell types, indicating a possible regulation of stromal cells through its receptors, OSMR and LIFR (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from scRNAseq analysis and in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: CFU-F frequencies were significantly reduced when stromal cells were cultured under single-cell conditions in comparison with bulk-cultured cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, CFU-F frequencies were significantly reduced when stromal cells were cultured under single-cell conditions in comparison with bulk-cultured cells, suggesting the presence of inter- and intra-stromal signaling among stromal cells.
evidence: This is a finding from functional assays.

claim: Multiple stimulatory pathways were operative between different stromal subsets as well as within the same stromal cell population.
source: Indeed, multiple stimulatory pathways were operative between different stromal subsets as well as within the same stromal cell population (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: FGF receptor-mediated signaling and various collagen-involving pathways were identified that reflected interactions between different stromal cells.
source: Among them, FGF receptor-mediated signaling and various collagen-involving pathways were identified that reflected interactions between different stromal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: CXCL12-, MDK-, GRN-, NRP1-, and BST2- mediated interactions were found to significantly contribute to the regulatory mechanisms of stromal cells.
source: In addition, CXCL12-, MDK-, GRN-, NRP1-, and BST2- mediated interactions were also found to significantly contribute to the regulatory mechanisms of stromal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: The endothelial cluster had a broad interaction spectrum with all hematopoietic clusters.
source: As illustrated in Figure 7A, the endothelial cluster had a broad interaction spectrum with all hematopoietic clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: The endothelial cluster interacted with hematopoietic clusters mainly through HLA molecules-, TNFRSF family members- and LGALS9-mediated interactions.
source: In addition to the endothelial-specific SELL-SELPLG and ICAM3-aLb2 complex pathways, it was predicted that the endothelial cluster interacted with hematopoietic clusters mainly through HLA molecules-, TNFRSF family members- and LGALS9-mediated interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: CXCL12-mediated interactions were not identified as the main signaling pathways in the crosstalk between endothelial cells and hematopoietic cells.
source: Unlike stromal cells, CXCL12-mediated interactions were not identified as the main signaling pathways in the crosstalk between endothelial cells and hematopoietic cells, indicating that endothelial cells and stromal cells communicate with hematopoietic cells through different mechanisms.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: The low frequency of BM stromal stem/progenitor cells (around 0.001–0.01% of BM cells) imposed challenges to detect CXCL12-expressing stromal cells in the CD45low/-CD235a- population.
source: The well-known low frequency of the BM stromal stem/progenitor cells (around 0.001–0.01% of BM cells) (Pittenger et al., 1999) imposed challenges to detect CXCL12-expressing stromal cells in the CD45low/-CD235a- population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and explains the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ cells are highly enriched for CXCL12-expressing BM stromal stem and progenitor cells.
source: In order to also capture and be able to analyze extremely rare stromal cell subsets, we therefore also sorted CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ cells, which are highly enriched for CXCL12-expressing BM stromal stem and progenitor cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Tormin et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and explains the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The CD271+ cell enrichment strategy validated that a high-resolution transcriptomic analysis of the human BM stromal compartment would not have been achieved without CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ enrichment.
source: These findings thus validated our CD271+ cell enrichment strategy and proved that a high-resolution transcriptomic analysis of the thus far poorly defined human BM stromal compartment would not have been achieved without CD45low/-CD235a-CD271+ enrichment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the data.

claim: Corresponding murine stromal cell types have been reported for most of the human stromal cell types identified (MSSCs, HAGEPs, OCs, pre-osteoblasts, and pre-fibroblasts).
source: Of note, corresponding murine stromal cell types have been reported for most of these cell types (MSSCs, HAGEPs, OCs, pre-osteoblasts, and pre-fibroblasts), whereas the cluster annotated as balanced progenitors has not been described either in mice or in humans (Baryawno et al., 2019; Tikhonova et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The cluster annotated as balanced progenitors has not been described either in mice or in humans.
source: Of note, corresponding murine stromal cell types have been reported for most of these cell types (MSSCs, HAGEPs, OCs, pre-osteoblasts, and pre-fibroblasts), whereas the cluster annotated as balanced progenitors has not been described either in mice or in humans (Baryawno et al., 2019; Tikhonova et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Self-renewing human skeletal stem cells (hSSC) with osteogenic and chondrogenic potential have been previously identified in human fetal and adult bones based on the phenotype PDPN+CD146-CD73+CD164+.
source: Self-renewing human skeletal stem cells (hSSC) with osteogenic and chondrogenic potential have been previously identified in human fetal and adult bones based on the phenotype PDPN+CD146-CD73+CD164+ (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The identity of a tri-lineage multipotent stromal progenitor in adult human bone marrow was not reported prior to this study.
source: However, the identity of a tri-lineage multipotent stromal progenitor in adult human bone marrow was not reported.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The study provides a phenotypical definition that allows for the faithful identification and prospective isolation of molecularly defined stromal stem and progenitors from hematopoietically active adult bone marrow.
source: Herein, we were able to provide a phenotypical definition that allowed for the faithful identification and prospective isolation of molecularly defined stromal stem and progenitors from hematopoietically active adult bone marrow.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings of the study.

claim: The data complement and extend reported phenotype definitions of MSCs from bone marrow and skeletal tissues.
source: These cells have thus far remained incompletely characterized and our data thus complement and extend reported phenotype definitions of MSCs from bone marrow and skeletal tissues (Jones et al., 2002; Quirici et al., 2002; Gronthos et al., 2007; Sacchetti et al., 2007; Delorme et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The phenotypic MSSCs defined in this study showed expression of previously reported stromal surface markers such as CD51 and CD146.
source: The phenotypic MSSCs defined in this study also showed expression of previously reported stromal surface markers such as CD51 (Pinho and Frenette, 2019) and CD146 (Tormin et al., 2011; data not shown).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: scRNAseq identified VCAN as a potentially important stromal gene based on its high expression in stromal clusters.
source: Besides these surface markers, scRNAseq also identified VCAN as a potentially important stromal gene based on its high expression in stromal clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: VCAN is not an optimal marker to isolate viable stromal cells because it is an extracellular matrix protein and is also expressed by monocytes.
source: However, as an extracellular matrix protein, FACS analysis of cellular VCAN expression can only be achieved based on its intracellular expression after fixation and permeabilization. Additionally, VCAN is also expressed by monocytes (cluster 36). Therefore, VCAN is not an optimal marker to isolate viable stromal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the properties of VCAN and the experimental data.

claim: The study performed a preliminary analysis which indicated possible age- and gender-related stromal differences.
source: Furthermore, we performed a preliminary analysis which indicated possible age- and gender-related stromal differences as also reported for murine cells (Singh et al., 2016; Maryanovich et al., 2018; Aguilar-Navarro et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The findings on age- and gender-related stromal differences need to be confirmed by additional experimentation in forthcoming studies.
source: However, this potentially interesting finding needs to be confirmed by additional experimentation in forthcoming studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Elegant studies in mice using genetic approaches have provided detailed insight into the functional roles of stromal cells in regulating hematopoiesis.
source: In mice, elegant studies using genetic approaches involving in-vivo labelling of cell types and ablation of candidate niche cells and niche factors have provided detailed insight into the functional roles of stromal cells in regulating hematopoiesis (Pinho and Frenette, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Comparable studies to those in mice are impossible to perform in humans.
source: Comparable studies in human are impossible to perform and analysis of human stromal cells function has been limited to in-vitro models.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of human research.

claim: Analysis of human stromal cell function has been limited to in-vitro models.
source: Comparable studies in human are impossible to perform and analysis of human stromal cells function has been limited to in-vitro models.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of human research.

claim: Stromal cells generally showed hematopoiesis supporting potential, which is consistent with previously published in-vitro coculture data.
source: We therefore investigated cellular interactions based on ligand-receptor interactions and found a broad and complicated crosstalk network, which is likely to reflect – at least in part – the in-situ situation as data were generated with directly isolated cells. We found that stromal cells generally showed hematopoiesis supporting potential, which is consistent with previously published in-vitro coculture data (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020) and which we confirmed in co-cultures with BM CD34+ cells and MSSC- or OC-derived stromal feeder cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and experimental data.

claim: Cell-cell interaction mechanisms differed considerably between different groups of stromal cell groups.
source: Furthermore, whereas all stromal cell groups showed the potential to interact with almost all hematopoietic cells, cell-cell interaction mechanisms differed considerably between different groups of stromal cell groups, that is between group A/C cells which included the MSSCs and group B cells (OCs).
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Group A/C cells demonstrated the potential to interact with hematopoiesis through cytokines such as CXCL12, IL7, KITLG, MDK, and TF as well as adhesion molecules providing direct cell-to-cell contact (e.g. VCAM1).
source: Whereas the former demonstrated the potential to interact with hematopoiesis through cytokines such as CXCL12, IL7, KITLG, MDK, and TF as well as adhesion molecules providing direct cell-to-cell contact (e.g. VCAM1), SPP1-mediated interactions were predicted to be the main pathways for the latter.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: SPP1-mediated interactions were predicted to be the main pathways for group B cells (OCs).
source: Whereas the former demonstrated the potential to interact with hematopoiesis through cytokines such as CXCL12, IL7, KITLG, MDK, and TF as well as adhesion molecules providing direct cell-to-cell contact (e.g. VCAM1), SPP1-mediated interactions were predicted to be the main pathways for the latter.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: Hematopoietic cells were maintained by different stromal populations through diverse but stromal cell-specific pathways.
source: These results thus indicated that hematopoietic cells were maintained by different stromal populations through diverse but nevertheless stromal cell-specific pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: SPP1-expressing OCs were located endosteally and CD271 single positive stromal cells including MSSCs were localized in the perivascular and stromal regions.
source: Taking furthermore into account that SPP1-expressing OCs were located endosteally and that CD271 single positive stromal cells including MSSCs were localized in the perivascular and stromal regions, respectively, suggested the possibility that different stromal cells provide specialized niches for hematopoietic cells in different locations.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ localization analysis.

claim: Different stromal cells provide specialized niches for hematopoietic cells in different locations.
source: Taking furthermore into account that SPP1-expressing OCs were located endosteally and that CD271 single positive stromal cells including MSSCs were localized in the perivascular and stromal regions, respectively, suggested the possibility that different stromal cells provide specialized niches for hematopoietic cells in different locations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and interaction data.

claim: The data confirm and extend previous reports describing that endosteal and perivascular niches exist in human BM.
source: Our data thus confirm and extend previous reports describing that endosteal and perivascular niches exist in human BM (Tormin et al., 2011; Pinho et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The data conceptually support a model where different hematopoietic cell types are differentially regulated by distinct niche milieus which are composed of specific cytokine-producing stromal cells.
source: and conceptually support a model where different hematopoietic cell types are differentially regulated by distinct niche milieus which are composed of specific cytokine-producing stromal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: In silico ligand-receptor interaction predictions suggested that endothelial cells and stromal cells showed the potential to communicate with hematopoiesis through different mechanisms.
source: Finally, in silico ligand-receptor interaction predictions suggested that endothelial cells and stromal cells showed the potential to communicate with hematopoiesis through different mechanisms, which is certainly an interesting finding that needs to be further addressed in future studies.
evidence: This is a finding from in silico cell-cell communication analysis.

claim: The study used human BM aspiration samples in which bone-lining or bone-attaching cells are most likely underrepresented.
source: In this study, we used human BM aspiration samples in which bone-lining or bone-attaching cells are most likely underrepresented.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The experiments could be complemented by studies on fresh bone marrow biopsy samples from healthy individuals.
source: Our experiments could therefore ideally be complemented by studies on fresh bone marrow biopsy samples from healthy individuals, which however were not available to us, and which might be difficult to acquire because of ethical considerations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Tri-lineage differentiation capacities of stromal clusters were evaluated using standard in-vitro assays, which may not necessarily reflect the bona fide stromal cell potentials.
source: In our study, tri-lineage differentiation capacities of stromal clusters were evaluated using standard in-vitro assays, which may not necessarily reflect the bona fide stromal cell potentials.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The data need to be complemented in follow-up studies by in vivo differentiation studies, for example using humanized BM ossicles.
source: Thus, these data need to be complemented in follow-up studies by in vivo differentiation studies, for example using humanized BM ossicles.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for research.

claim: The potential key genes that govern the stromal cell fate commitment were predicted using likelihood-based computation.
source: The potential key genes that govern the stromal cell fate commitment were predicted using likelihood-based computation and the stroma-hematopoiesis crosstalk mechanisms were inferred based on ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence: This describes the analytical methods used in the study.

claim: The stroma-hematopoiesis crosstalk mechanisms were inferred based on ligand-receptor interactions.
source: The potential key genes that govern the stromal cell fate commitment were predicted using likelihood-based computation and the stroma-hematopoiesis crosstalk mechanisms were inferred based on ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence: This describes the analytical methods used in the study.

claim: The identified key genes and interactions will need to be validated in future experiments.
source: The identified key genes and interactions will need to be validated in future experiments, for example using in vitro engineered human BM models or in vivo humanized BM ossicles (Dupard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for research.

claim: The CellPhoneDB analysis predicted the communication networks between stromal and hematopoietic cells without considering the spatial proximity of the cells and functional relevance of the interaction.
source: While the CellPhoneDB analysis predicted the communication networks between stromal and hematopoietic cells, this approach infers potential interactions using transcriptomics data without considering the spatial proximity of the cells and functional relevance of the interaction.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analytical approach.

claim: A more comprehensive overview of cellular communication is anticipated when combined with spatial localization analysis and functional assays in future studies.
source: A more comprehensive overview of cellular communication is anticipated when combined with spatial localization analysis and functional assays in future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for research.

claim: The results provide the basis for a better understanding of the cellular complexity of the human BM microenvironment.
source: Despite these limitations, we believe that our results provide the basis for a better understanding of the cellular complexity of the human BM microenvironment and put a new light on the current concept that specialized niches exist for distinct types of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Morrison and Scadden, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: The results put a new light on the current concept that specialized niches exist for distinct types of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: Despite these limitations, we believe that our results provide the basis for a better understanding of the cellular complexity of the human BM microenvironment and put a new light on the current concept that specialized niches exist for distinct types of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Morrison and Scadden, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings supported by a citation.
